text: On November 4, 2026, an Ask HN thread asked developers for their current AI agent setup, and 663 comments came back. We read every one, counted the tools 424 people say they use, and turned the most detailed setups into seven patterns you can start using today. On November 4, 2026, the user eggbrain posted "Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?" It asked five questions: which AI plans people pay for, which other models they use, which coding harness (the program that runs the agent) they use, whether they use tools that run many agents at once, and whether they use always-on agent platforms. We fetched the thread on November 6, 2026, at about 9:00 AM MST. It had 534 points and 663 comments from 530 different people. 392 comments were direct answers to the post. The rest were replies. Three readers each read every comment. For each one they wrote down the tools the person says they use, the tools they only mention, and any signs of an advanced setup, such as parallel agents or a review loop. We then counted people, not comments, so a person who posted five times counts once per tool. All the links for tools and comments named on this page are in the Sources list at the bottom. These are people who say they use each tool, out of the 424 commenters who named at least one. One person can use many tools, so the numbers add up to more than 424. When someone said Claude while talking about coding, the readers counted it as Claude Code. Counted November 6, 2026. Tool (what it is) People Claude Code (Anthropic coding agent) 180 Claude plan (Pro, Max or Team) 145 Codex (OpenAI coding agent) 103 ChatGPT plan or app 92 Claude Opus (model) 80 DeepSeek (open-weight models) 78 OpenCode (open-source coding agent) 69 Pi (open-source coding agent) 67 OpenRouter (one API for many models) 55 Qwen (open-weight models) 46 GLM from Z.ai (open-weight models) 44 Gemini (Google models and app) 36 Hermes Agent (personal agent) 29 Herdr (runs many agent sessions) 28 GPT models through the API 26 VS Code (editor) 26 GitHub Copilot 22 Claude Sonnet (model) 19 Grok (models and app) 17 tmux (terminal multiplexer) 17 Antigravity (Google agent IDE) 17 Claude Code is the most used agent by a wide margin, but most of its users run something else too. Only 73 of its 180 users named no other coding agent, and 67 people use both Claude Code and Codex. Open-source agents are not far behind. OpenCode (69 people) and Pi (67) each have close to twice the users of Gemini (36) and three to four times those of GitHub Copilot (22) or Cursor (16). Cheap open-weight models carry real load. DeepSeek (78 people) is named almost as often as Claude Opus (80), and two of the setups below use it as their main builder model. Running many agents needs a tool to watch them. Herdr (28 people) and tmux (17) are the most common ways people here keep track of which session needs them. Nine setups worth studying We picked these because each one shows a pattern clearly and gives enough detail to copy. We re-read each full comment. The setups are as the commenters describe them; we did not test them. What it is: each task gets its own folder and branch, made with git worktree, and its own agent session. Agents cannot overwrite each other's files, and you merge each branch when it is ready. Why it helps: an agent often works for minutes at a time, so one agent means a lot of waiting. Our readers tagged 105 people as running agents in parallel. The top comment in the thread, from thefourthchime, says to keep at least five things going so you are not sitting around for one agent. # one folder and branch per task git worktree add ../myapp-login -b fix-login git worktree add ../myapp-search -b add-search # or let Claude Code make the worktree and start a session in it claude --worktree fix-login Tools: git worktree, Claude Code's --worktree option, and a session manager that shows which agent needs you, such as Herdr (28 people), tmux (17), Zellij, Orca, Paseo or T3 Code. paustint and skwee357 run this every day. Watch out: glennfiedler warns that code written by many models working alone can come out as a patchwork that needs a cleanup pass. Start with two or three agents and add more when review keeps up. What it is: when the builder finishes, a second agent with no memory of the build reads the diff and lists real problems. It can be a new subagent of the same model or a model from another vendor. Fix, then review again. Why it helps: the agent that wrote the code tends to trust its own work. Our readers tagged 56 people with a review loop. KronisLV loops until nothing serious remains, gregwebs gives the reviewer job to Codex, and glennfiedler says each model sees things the others miss. # a read-only second opinion from a different model # (codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox by default) codex exec "Review the changes on this branch against main. List real bugs and missing tests only." # inside Claude Code, ask for a reviewer with a clean context > Start a new subagent with no context from this session. Have it review the diff against main and report only serious problems. Fix them, then review again. Tools: Codex non-interactive mode (codex exec), Claude Code subagents, GitHub Copilot code review on PRs, and Herdr, which lets one agent start another in the background with a command such as hc run --bg codex. enesalatas fires the Codex review from a Claude Code hook so it never gets skipped. What it is: the expensive model writes the plan and the tests that prove it. A cheaper model follows the plan. If the cheap model fails, the task moves up to a stronger one. Why it helps: most of the tokens go into building, not planning. Our readers tagged 75 people as routing work by model. gregwebs keeps a three-model setup under $100 a month this way, and glennfiedler's coordinator moves a failed card up a tier instead of retrying the same model. # 1. the strong model writes the plan, no code claude -p "Write a step-by-step plan for <task> in PLAN.md, with the tests that prove it works. Do not write code." --allowedTools "Read,Write" # 2. a cheaper model builds from PLAN.md in an open agent such as OpenCode or Pi # 3. if the tests still fail after two tries, hand the same plan to the strong model Tools: OpenCode and Pi, which can use many models; OpenRouter for one API across vendors; DeepSeek, GLM and Qwen as builder models. Watch out: the same glennfiedler who runs four tiers says one strong model at medium effort covers almost all of their work. Route by price only after the plain setup works. What it is: turn off permission prompts only inside a VM or container that holds the project and nothing else: no SSH keys, no API keys, and only the network the task needs. Keep strict limits outside the box. Why it helps: approving every command is slow, but an agent with full access to your laptop can do real damage. Our readers tagged 67 people as using a sandbox, VM or container. thefunnyman notes that "most folks don't think much about isolation." # Docker Sandboxes: run Claude Code in an isolated sandbox with your project sbx run claude ~/my-project # Lima: a throwaway Linux VM on a Mac brew install lima limactl start Tools: Docker Sandboxes, Lima, Docker. Two extras from the thread: give each box an egress allowlist, as enesalatas does, and add a hook that blocks risky actions, the way phillc73 blocks a remote git push until they approve it. Claude Code hooks can do this. What it is: before the agent starts, write a short spec and a definition of done. Keep standing rules in an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md file that every session reads. Why it helps: an agent that knows where the finish line is stops at the right place and checks its own work. Our readers tagged 33 people as writing specs or plans first and 31 as using memory files. thefourthchime says the biggest trick is to "tell it what complete looks like." cpobuda does not start coding until the spec is clear. ## Definition of done (put this in AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md) - All tests pass: npm test - New behavior has a test that failed before the change - No new dependencies without asking - The final message lists the files changed and how to check the work Tools: AGENTS.md, Claude Code's CLAUDE.md memory, and Claude Code skills for steps you repeat. What it is: run the agent with no chat window, from a script, a cron job or CI. It starts from an issue or ticket and ends with a pull request that a person reviews. Why it helps: routine fixes stop waiting on you to type the first message. Our readers tagged 40 people with headless or CI agents. sudhirj turns GitHub issues into one-shot Claude runs, steveridout runs Claude and Codex through a pipeline of bug repro, build, review and QA, and dgunay has a coordinator agent turn tickets into tasks for workers that must pass an agent review before they see the PR. 0xbadcafebee gives these agents read-only credentials made just for the job. # Claude Code, non-interactive claude -p "Read issue #123 with gh, fix it on a new branch, run the tests, and open a draft PR" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash" # Codex, non-interactive, allowed to edit files in the workspace codex exec --sandbox workspace-write "Fix the failing test in tests/test_auth.py, then run the tests" Tools: Claude Code headless mode (claude -p), Codex non-interactive mode (codex exec), and Beads for tracking agent tasks. Run these inside the box from pattern 4. What it is: the agent runs on a desk machine or a server, and you answer its questions, approve steps and steer it from your phone. Why it helps: long runs often stall while waiting for a yes. Our readers tagged 60 people with remote or phone control. sudhirj works from the Claude app on phone and iPad, and gregwebs reaches their agents over Tailscale. # in your project, then open the session from the Claude app on your phone claude remote-control # or a plain terminal: Tailscale on both devices, then mosh in (Blink Shell on iOS) mosh you@your-desk-machine Tools: Claude Code Remote Control, Tailscale, mosh, Blink Shell, and Orca and Paseo, which both have mobile apps.
